content: Diabetes mellitus is associated with a range of cardiovascular complications, which can be categorized into microvascular and macrovascular diseases. Microvascular complications include diabetic retinopathy, neuropathy, and nephropathy, while macrovascular complications encompass coronary artery disease and stroke. Chronic hyperglycemia in diabetes leads to damage to blood vessels, a condition known as angiopathy. Endothelial cells lining the blood vessels absorb excess glucose because they are not dependent on insulin for glucose uptake. This results in the overproduction of surface glycoproteins, causing the basement membrane of the blood vessels to become abnormally thickened and weakened. The vascular damage in diabetes is classified into microvascular disease, which affects small blood vessels, and macrovascular disease, which impacts larger arteries. Microvascular Disease Damage to small blood vessels results in microangiopathy, which can manifest in several ways: Diabetic retinopathy: This condition involves the growth of fragile, low-quality new blood vessels in the retina, as well as macular edema (swelling of the macula). These changes can lead to significant vision loss or even blindness. Retinal damage caused by microangiopathy is the leading cause of blindness among non-elderly adults in the United States. Diabetic neuropathy: This refers to abnormal or reduced sensation, often presenting in a glove and stocking distribution, starting in the feet and potentially progressing to the fingers and hands. When combined with vascular damage, diabetic neuropathy can contribute to the development of diabetic foot. Other forms of diabetic neuropathy may present as mononeuritis or autonomic neuropathy. Diabetic amyotrophy, a specific form of neuropathy, results in muscle weakness. Diabetic nephropathy: This involves damage to the kidneys, which can progress to chronic renal failure, eventually necessitating dialysis. Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of adult kidney failure in developed countries. Macrovascular Disease Macrovascular complications in diabetes lead to cardiovascular disease, with accelerated atherosclerosis being a major contributing factor: Coronary artery disease: This can result in angina or myocardial infarction (commonly known as a heart attack). Stroke: Ischemic strokes are the predominant type associated with diabetes. Peripheral vascular disease: This condition contributes to intermittent claudication (pain in the legs and feet during exertion) and diabetic foot. Diabetic foot often arises from a combination of neuropathy and arterial disease, leading to skin ulcers, infections, and, in severe cases, necrosis and gangrene. This explains why individuals with diabetes are more prone to leg and foot infections and why their wounds in these areas take longer to heal. Diabetic foot is the leading cause of adult amputations, typically involving the toes or feet, in developed countries. Interestingly, carotid artery stenosis does not occur more frequently in individuals with diabetes, and there is a lower prevalence of abdominal aortic aneurysm. However, diabetes is associated with higher morbidity, mortality, and operative risks in these conditions. Cardiovascular Disease and Gender Population-based studies indicate that men generally have a higher risk of cardiovascular disorders. However, women with diabetes face a disproportionately higher risk of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular disorders compared to men with diabetes. This increased risk in women appears to be independent of menopausal status. Contributing factors may include a higher proportion of fat tissue and a hyperactive immune system in women with diabetes.
